issue_context.title: Watchdog service broken for drivers without WDIOC_SETTIMEOUT support
issue_context.body:
**systemd version the issue has been seen with**
 > 247..main

<!-- **NOTE:** Do not submit bug reports about anything but the two most recently released *major* systemd versions upstream! -->
<!--           If there have been multiple stable releases for that major version, please consider updating to a recent one before reporting an issue. -->
<!--           When using a distro package, please make sure that the version reported is meaningful for upstream. -->
<!-- See https://github.com/systemd/systemd-stable/releases for the list of most recent releases. -->
<!-- For older version please use distribution trackers (see https://systemd.io/CONTRIBUTING#filing-issues). -->

**Used distribution**
 > Debian 11

**Linux kernel version used** (`uname -a`)
<!-- Make sure to enclose the pasted kernel version in `backticks`, so that
     GitHub doesn't convert the `#` character typically included in it into a
     reference to old GitHub issues. -->
 > `Linux iot2050-debian 5.14.0+ #183 SMP PREEMPT Thu Sep 9 08:26:49 CEST 2021 aarch64 GNU/Linux`
 > This is a custom kernel, but watchdog driver (rti-wdt) is upstream

**CPU architecture issue was seen on**
 > arm64

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**
 > systemd drives watchdog according to the specified RuntimeWatchdogSec period, even if (re-)setting that timeout failes with `EOPNOTSUPP`.

**Unexpected behaviour you saw**
 > Watchdog is not pinged by systemd. System resets after the programmed timeout of the watchdog, either set via `rti_wdt.hearbeat` (kernel command line) or by the bootloader that already started the watchdog.

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
 > On our device (https://github.com/siemens/meta-iot2050/), by patching an existing watchdog driver to drop `WDIOF_SETTIMEOUT`, or by faking `EOPNOTSUPP` in `update_timeout()` (`src/shared/watchdog.c`) for `WDIOC_SETTIMEOUT`

**Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue**

<!-- Please paste relevant program terminal or journal output here, ideally
     when generated in debug mode (try setting the SYSTEMD_LOG_LEVEL=debug
     environment variable). For very long copy/pasted data consider using a
     service like https://gist.github.com/. Where copy/paste is not possible
     (for example early boot or late shutdown), a photo of the screen might do
     too, but text is always much preferred. -->
```text
Sep 09 09:56:27 iot2050-debian systemd[1]: Using hardware watchdog 'K3 RTI Watchdog', version 0, device /dev/watchdog
Sep 09 09:56:27 iot2050-debian systemd[1]: Failed to set timeout to 600s: Operation not supported
...
```

This used to work - more or less by chance - up to 61927b9f116bf45bfdbf19dc2981d4a4f527ae5f which now only considers the watchdog started when the timeout was successfully set. And only a started watchdog is pinged since then.
comments: FWIW, the kernel rejected a workaround: https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/4d82b8ce-bc34-e4b2-c5fe-9e883b0db59d@siemens.com (we will still carry this locally for now - easier than keeping a patched systemd for Debian)

It may make sense to fallback to the timeout used by the device if it returns -EOPNOTSUPP with WDIOC_SETTIMEOUT in any cases. However it seems awkward to configure a (arbitrary) timeout value in system.conf to support this case (ie open the watchdog and reuse the driver value). 

Maybe we could introduce a new kernel command line option to support this specific case ?

Something like `systemd.watchdog_start[=timeout]` which would take an optional timeout parameter. The parameter would specify the desired timeout value in sec. If the parameter is not passed then it would reuse the driver value.

> It may make sense to fallback to the timeout used by the device if it returns -EOPNOTSUPP with WDIOC_SETTIMEOUT in any cases. However it seems awkward to configure a (arbitrary) timeout value in system.conf to support this case (ie open the watchdog and reuse the driver value).

I wouldn't see it that way: setting a timeout is "best effort" stuff, i.e. you get the timeout if we can set it, and if we don#t you dont. And even if we are able to set it then very likely you'll actually just get a timeout close to what you asked for, given hw limitations.

> Maybe we could introduce a new kernel command line option to support this specific case ?
> 
> Something like `systemd.watchdog_start[=timeout]` which would take an optional timeout parameter. The parameter would specify the desired timeout value in sec. If the parameter is not passed then it would reuse the driver value.

I amnot sure I follow what this has to do with drivers that lack WDIOC_SETTIMEOUT?

I mean, adding such a kernel cmdline option sounds ok, but it appears to me has little to do with wether the driver supports setting the timeout or not.

> I amnot sure I follow what this has to do with drivers that lack WDIOC_SETTIMEOUT?

Indeed that's unrelated. I think the option would be only useful for debugging purposes or in the case the watchdog would be started by the bootloader and the timeout value would be too small to have enough time to instruct PID1 to ping the device.

review_comments: Not if we want to keep the assert right before: `assert(ntime >= watchdog_last_ping);`

given how shitty drivers are maybe validate the value they return. i.e. an assert() probably is sufficient, that encodes are API assumptions here:

```c
assert(sec > 0);
```

hmm an assert would crash PID1.

Wouldn't it be better to assume that the passed timeout value has been used by the driver (since it returned 0) instead ?

Well, we use assert()s to catch programming errors, and encode API assumptions. 

If the driver actually returns WDIOC_SETTIMEOUT zero in the timeout parameter here, that's a bug in the driver, and if the driver is buggy i think it's OK if we fail too. 

I mean, this is mostly a theoretical issue, if all drivers work correctly this should never happen. 

Or to say this differently: hitting an assert() if a driver breaks our assumptions and is broken is better than busy looping because we trigger the timeout continously in our event loop.

Adding an error path that tries to handle this issue gracefully is too mucht i think, because we are not actually aware of any driver actually returning rubbish here.

if we go this way, then watchdog_set_timeout() should be renamed to watchdog_start() (or watchdog_setup(), or watchdog_prepare()) or so (since it suddenly is not just a boring setter, but the "constructor", that *must* be called, for anything to actually happen), but still take the timeout arg.
Also, this commit as it stands now will break shutdown.c, since we don't call watchdog_set_timeout() there at all.
